title: Moscow Under Siege
subtitle: Emergency defence measures and the continuing crisis around Moscow.
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: Moscow’s state of siege assigns military responsibilities, restricts movement and authorises summary force while the city remains unencircled.
body:
An order before it took effect

The order announced on 19 October named three men and three responsibilities: Zhukov would defend Moscow's western approaches, Pavel Artemev its near approaches, and Kuzma Sinilov order within the city. From 20 October, Moscow and adjoining districts were to be under a state of siege. The State Defence Committee was responding to a military threat and to the disorder surrounding evacuation, but the capital had not been encircled. “Siege” here designated an emergency regime of government. Its provisions joined the work of defending the city to a system of passes, patrols, military tribunals and summary force. [1][2]

The problem inherited from 16 October was not that the government had simply fled and left an empty capital. Some state offices and the diplomatic corps had been directed towards Kuibyshev, while Stalin remained and the army continued to defend outside the city. The problem was whether a government in partial transit, a population alarmed by its departure and a front assembled from damaged forces could still act together. The decree gave a formal answer: name commanders for the outer and inner defences, regulate movement at night and give security forces authority to impose order. Those provisions did not establish that each military sector was secure or each resident reassured. They show what the leadership thought had to be made governable.[3][2][4]

Moscow had not been surrounded. A German force north of the capital, another pressing from the west and a panzer army approaching from the southwest posed a combined threat, but the line between them was neither a completed encirclement nor a single front of equal strength. The official declaration itself said that defence was being conducted roughly 100–120 kilometres west of the city. That distance was a public characterisation of the crisis, not a surveyed radius applicable to every sector. Some German units were nearer particular towns, others still fought behind the farthest spearheads, and Soviet strongpoints interrupted the approaches. The city could be gravely threatened without being taken or even immediately encircled.[2][4]

Outer front and inner defence

The order distinguished two military responsibilities. Georgy Zhukov commanded the Western Front forces defending the outer approaches. Lieutenant General Pavel Artemev, identified in the translation as chief of the Moscow garrison, held responsibility for the near approaches. Major General Kuzma Sinilov, the Moscow commandant, was charged with order in the city. These were overlapping layers of defence and governance, not three rival commanders each directing the entire battle. Their separation reflects a practical fact: the person assigning divisions on the Mozhaisk road could not also direct every curfew pass, urban patrol and antiaircraft movement. The government attempted to make the chain of command legible before an emergency could collapse it.[2]

Zhukov's command had already changed as the threat widened. He had taken over the combined Western and Reserve Fronts on 10 October; on the seventeenth, the Stavka created Kalinin Front under Ivan Konev to handle the northern flank. The new command responded to the danger exposed by Kalinin's fall three days earlier. It separated a northern battle from the direct western approaches while keeping both within the defence of the capital. These arrangements show a command structure being adapted during a crisis. The state of siege was another layer in that adaptation, allocating responsibility inside Moscow while front headquarters directed armies beyond it. [4]

The German force moving through the Kalinin direction had captured that city on 14 October. That success threatened northern connections and encouraged fear in Moscow, but the subsequent front still required German troops to move across country, secure roads and defeat Soviet forces that could counterattack from the flank. On the western routes, positions around Volokolamsk and Mozhaisk offered Soviet commanders places to hold the principal road corridors. Farther south, the approaches through Kaluga and towards Tula forced German units to spread their effort. The term “under siege” in the Soviet decree therefore described a regime of emergency authority within Moscow; it should not be taken as a military map claiming that a German siege ring had closed around the city.[4][2]

The decree explicitly connected emergency authority with support for the defending forces. Its restrictions were intended to make a functioning military base out of a city disrupted by evacuation. Control of street movement mattered because soldiers, supplies and civilian traffic shared the same routes. Protection of depots and communications mattered because the front still depended on them. The measure did not suspend urban life altogether: it created exceptions for authorised people and vehicles and referred air-alert movement to separate instructions. Moscow was to remain inhabited and productive, but activity within it would increasingly depend on permissions enforced by the garrison and security services. [2]

Unrest was not confined to Moscow. On 19 October, workers in Ivanovo attacked administrative and Party premises and officials, according to Mark Edele's account. Some raised the demand for soviets without Communists: a challenge to Party authority expressed through the language of Soviet institutions. This was a civilian disturbance, not an army mutiny, and it belongs to Ivanovo rather than to a count of incidents in the capital. It nevertheless reveals a tension in wartime mobilisation. A state requiring continued labour and sacrifice could encounter opposition from the very workers in whose name it claimed to govern. The Moscow decree attempted to contain disorder locally within that wider political crisis. [5]

Artemev's responsibility for the near approaches joined the field defence to the capital's own garrison. If units withdrew from an outer position, they needed a continuing command structure behind them; if an enemy penetration reached closer to Moscow, someone had to organise resistance beyond the responsibilities of the front armies. The decree established that division of labour but did not certify that every planned position was complete. Its importance lay in allocating authority before the emergency became still more acute. The government was preparing for possible military failure without conceding that the city must be abandoned. [2][4]

Three named responsibilities

The 19 October decree assigned the western front to Zhukov, the near approaches to Artemev and street order to Sinilov. The distinction is a guide to the crisis: defending the capital required field armies, a garrison and a functioning city administration, each with different tasks.[2]

Curfew, passes and coercion

From midnight until five in the morning, people and vehicles were forbidden to move without a special pass. During an air alert, separate published instructions applied. The hours and exemptions show the character of the regime more clearly than the general phrase “martial law.” It aimed to distinguish authorised movement from movement the authorities could stop and investigate. The distinction was enforceable only because patrols could demand papers and impose consequences. A resident's ordinary freedom to travel was subordinated to the city's emergency administration, while essential work and military transport continued through the permit system. [2]

Sinilov could call on the NKVD's internal troops, the civilian police and volunteer workers' detachments. The NKVD, the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs, combined security and policing functions with armed formations. The decree ordered military tribunals to deal rapidly with violations of public order. For those designated provocateurs, spies or enemy agents disturbing order, it prescribed shooting on the spot. This was an authorisation for summary killing, not simply an expedited trial procedure. Its categories also placed considerable power in the hands of those identifying a suspect. The order supplied no list of proven offenders and no total of executions under its provisions. [2]

The decree's language cannot establish that the preceding unrest was organised by enemy agents. Edele's evidence of attacks on officials and antisemitic crowd violence identifies conduct requiring explanation on its own terms. Steinhardt's reports described disorder and declining morale, not a demonstrated German conspiracy behind every incident. A state seeking to suppress opposition had an interest in identifying threats through security categories, especially when evacuation had exposed divisions between officials and residents. The historian can recognise the danger of sabotage without accepting official labels as findings of guilt. For any individual execution, the order alone is evidence of authorised power, not proof of the victim's conduct. [5][6][2]

It would be equally mistaken to portray the state of siege as only a repressive gesture detached from defence. Army headquarters needed their routes protected, and a breakdown in distribution or transport could harm soldiers at the front and residents within Moscow. The issue is that emergency regulation served these functions through institutions able to compel and punish. Civilians were asked to keep working and to assist the Red Army while accepting restrictions on movement and the risk of being treated as an enemy if they challenged authority. To understand the decree is to hold both parts of that fact together. The state's practical needs do not excuse indiscriminate violence; the presence of coercion does not make the danger to the city imaginary.[2][4]

The division between military and police responsibilities also placed limits on what the decree itself could accomplish. Sinilov could regulate the city and use the forces assigned to him, but Zhukov and Konev still had to decide how to employ armies against the German approaches. Artemev's garrison linked the two spheres without replacing either front command. The arrangement mattered because the evacuation crisis could otherwise obscure where authority remained. A government institution leaving Moscow did not transfer command of the Western Front to Kuibyshev by default; a city patrol did not acquire responsibility for an army's withdrawal. The decree named responsibilities to prevent administrative movement from becoming a vacuum of power. Its coercive provisions made those responsibilities forceful, but their military success depended on cooperation between commands whose tasks and available means were different. The separation of roles was therefore part of the defence, as well as a statement about who would enforce the state's orders. [2][4]

Residents inside the new regime

The decree closed by appealing to workers to remain calm, assist the Red Army and help maintain order. The appeal was part of the same document that threatened summary force. This combination is revealing: the government sought active cooperation while reserving the means to compel it. Residents were being addressed as contributors to the defence and as subjects of emergency policing. The wording does not reveal how each person responded, but it does show what the leadership required from those who remained. Moscow had to keep supplying labour, material and organised support while its population lived with the prospect of a further German advance. [2][4][6]

Fortification labour gave that cooperation a physical form. The largely female workforce constructing the defensive belts had already contributed to the city's protection before the decree. Emergency administration now had to sustain the transport, food and organisation on which such work depended. Completed earthworks were only one component of defence: they needed troops, weapons and connection with neighbouring positions. Civilian effort could enlarge the options available to commanders, but it could not independently make up for the field armies' losses. The link between the home front and battle was therefore direct and demanding, with the value of the labour depending on the military system able to use it. [4]

The public was also receiving a new official account of the danger. The decree placed the fighting roughly 100–120 kilometres west of Moscow and named Zhukov as commander there. After weeks in which communiqués had offered little useful warning, this statement provided a recognisable framework for the crisis. It remained a broad public description rather than a report on every approach. The northern danger around Kalinin and the southern threat could not be reduced to the same distance from the capital. The government's message joined disclosure to reassurance: it acknowledged a near military emergency while presenting command, order and continued resistance as established responsibilities. [2][7]

A later diplomatic assessment helps establish what followed. On 26 October, Steinhardt reported that conditions had improved during the preceding three days, drawing in part on information from Llewellyn Thompson, who had remained in Moscow. He believed Stalin's presence had helped preserve authority while other institutions established themselves in Kuibyshev. This was an ambassador's judgment about political stability, not a statistical measure of popular confidence or an audit of police activity. It shows that the October disorder had not developed into the collapse he feared. It does not establish how much improvement resulted from the decree, from the military situation or from the restoration of ordinary services. [6]

Steinhardt made continued authority conditional on the government's ability to feed the population. That observation placed a material limit on coercion. A permit could regulate the movement of a food vehicle, and a patrol could guard a depot, but neither created the food being moved. The government had to maintain distribution while the rail system carried reinforcements and evacuated institutions. The city's continued functioning depended on that everyday provision as well as on the defence outside it. The ambassador's later report does not establish a particular shortage on 19 October; it identifies sustenance as an essential condition of the stability the authorities were trying to restore. [6][2]

The volunteer workers' detachments named in the decree connected civilian mobilisation with the enforcement of order. They were placed at Sinilov's disposal alongside internal troops and police. This was a different function from digging defences or joining a field formation: civilians were also expected to support authority within the city. The document does not specify how each detachment was recruited or deployed. It does, however, identify a mechanism by which the workforce became part of the emergency apparatus. The same social institutions that sustained production could be used to organise patrols and protection of facilities, extending the commandant's reach into urban life. [2][4]

The permit and air-alert provisions also reveal that several forms of authority had to coexist. The curfew could not simply override every other wartime instruction, because an air raid required its own rules for movement and shelter. The decree therefore referred residents to the separate published arrangements governing an alert. Its detail shows an administration attempting to preserve distinctions within an emergency rather than issuing one universal prohibition. Such distinctions mattered because the penalties for violating order were severe. Clear instructions were part of the practical obligation of the authorities imposing them, not an incidental convenience for the people expected to obey. [2][3]

The provision for shooting on the spot gave the regime its sharpest coercive edge. A person placed in the decree's enemy categories could be killed without the tribunal process specified for other violations. That power should neither be softened into routine discipline nor expanded into an invented number of deaths. The distinction between an order and its implementation is crucial here. Resolution 813 proves that the government authorised summary killing in the capital's emergency; it does not identify every person against whom that authority was used. Establishing particular cases requires further records, and the absence of such cases in this study does not establish that the power went unused. [2]

What the decree cannot count

Resolution 813 authorised a curfew, tribunals and immediate shooting for specified categories. It does not report how many people were stopped, prosecuted or killed under those provisions. A dated study should describe the powers without turning the text of an order into an invented outcome statistic.[2]

The fight outside the decree

German headquarters had already issued orders for a closer encirclement. Fourth Army's instructions of 16 October envisaged a movement around Moscow, stopping at the belt railway rather than sending troops into the city. Hoepner's Fourth Panzer Group, after pushing through the Mozhaisk and Kaluga approaches, began turning on 18 October to help open the northern side of that operation. Fourth Army also expected assistance from Guderian on its right. The pieces had to work together: infantry could not complete the planned enclosure merely because one armoured group had advanced. The continued defence on the southern approaches and the declining mobility of the leading formations made that cooperation increasingly difficult.[4]

The widening gap between the plan and the army's ability to move was visible in its columns. By the end of October's third week, the spearhead divisions of Fourth Panzer Group and Second Panzer Army stretched along twenty-five to thirty miles of road. Marching infantry could sometimes overtake the tanks. Third Panzer Group even considered sending tank crews forward on foot with local horse carts. The problem was more serious than a temporary reduction in speed. A formation distributed along such a route could have its leading infantry in contact while its artillery, fuel and repair vehicles remained far behind. German commanders still possessed substantial force, but concentrating it for the next attack had become a battle with distance and congestion.[4]

Soviet formations continued to impose costs. The Kalinin Front under Konev guarded the northern sector after its creation on the seventeenth. Zhukov's Western Front defended the direct approaches with troops of uneven quality, including pocket survivors and arriving reserves. On the southwest arc, Soviet positions between the German spearhead and Tula made Guderian's intended movement a future operation rather than a completed fact. A roadblock could compel deployment of artillery or infantry; a counterattack could make a commander hold a reserve instead of sending it farther east. Neither action necessarily restored the pre-October Soviet front. Their value was to consume German time and material while the defensive system near Moscow acquired more substance.[4][8]

German intelligence helped sustain ambitions that the formations struggled to execute. An army high-command memorandum of 16 October interpreted Soviet demolition and eastward movement as a general withdrawal intended to preserve cadres for new formations in the winter. It recommended pressing forward and giving motorised pursuit units priority for fuel, so that the retreating enemy would not escape. This was an assessment and a proposed response, not proof that the Soviet armies had ceased resisting. It encouraged pursuit at precisely the point when the defenders were rebuilding near Moscow and German columns were increasingly difficult to concentrate. The interpretation of enemy movement thus mattered alongside the physical condition of the roads. [8]

The German operation also carried a distinct policy towards Moscow's inhabitants. Hitler's 12 October instruction rejected accepting capitulation, envisaged exclusion of German troops from the city and directed that civilians trying to flee towards German lines be forced back with fire. Soviet emergency rule sought to retain control of a city the government still defended; the German plan sought to make the city's population bear the consequences of isolation while denying it food and refuge under German protection. Each policy requires scrutiny through its own orders and acts. Identifying the Soviet decree's summary powers does not lessen the responsibility of the German authorities for the violence their proposed conquest entailed. [2][8]

The mobility problem had already affected formations expected to exploit the Vyazma victory. Stahel's account records Fourth Army reporting on 14 October that motor vehicles could no longer move off the roads and that the SS division Das Reich had to continue its advance on foot. Its commander, Paul Hausser, was seriously wounded that day. These details concern a particular formation and report; they do not establish that every German vehicle had stopped. They show how an ostensibly mobile operation could continue through infantry fighting after its transport advantage had weakened. At the time Moscow's emergency regime was being prepared, the attackers were still dangerous but increasingly unable to employ their component forces in the manner the plan required. Soviet resistance remained necessary to turn that impairment into delay: troops advancing on foot still had to be opposed, and roads still had to be defended. [9]

What “siege” meant on this date

At the end of 19 October, Moscow remained connected to Soviet-held territory, and the emergency regime was about to take effect. The government had specified who would defend the approaches, who would command the near defence and who would police the city. It had also curtailed ordinary movement and authorised extraordinary punishment. These were concrete changes in how residents would live under the military threat. They were not evidence that the threat had been removed. The city's continuing resistance still depended on the field armies, supply and the work of those who remained within it. [1][2][6]

The date also refutes a simple ending to the previous chapter. The sixteenth's panic was not the fall of Moscow, but neither was the nineteenth a return to normal civic life. Officials were still moving, residents still worked within a threatened city, and military commanders still fought for each approach. The emergency decree formalised the government's attempt to coordinate these activities. It could direct traffic, impose a curfew and threaten punishment; it could not repair a damaged army on its own. A tribunal did not substitute for an antitank gun, and an order to remain calm did not produce fuel for a tank. The defence depended on political authority, military action and material supply functioning together.[2][4]

The capital's emergency joined political survival to military defence, but the wider war continued to threaten the resources on which both rested. In eastern Ukraine, German forces were approaching Kharkov, another major industrial and railway centre. The Soviet state was trying to preserve institutions in Moscow and productive capacity elsewhere under the pressure of simultaneous advances. On 19 October, it had retained the ability to direct that effort. The next test was whether its armies, transport and industrial evacuation could continue functioning as important cities farther south passed into enemy hands. [4]
